docs.title: Known vulnerabilities
docs.text:
[advisories] fails a workspace that locks a package with a known vulnerability, without running a second tool:

[advisories]
fail-on = "high"            # an advisory at or above high fails (the default)
known-exploited = "error"   # one in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog fails, whatever its severity
epss = 0.1                  # one FIRST rates 10% or more likely to be exploited in 30 days fails (off by default)

[advisories] on its own fails on high and critical advisories and on known exploited ones. Each finding names the advisory and its CVE, and the help names the version that fixes it:

error[advisories.vulnerable] urllib3 1.26.4: GHSA-v845-jxx5-vc9f (CVE-2023-43804), high severity: `Cookie` HTTP header isn't stripped on cross-origin redirects
  --> pixi.lock: environment "default", linux-64
  = help: upgrade to 1.26.17 or later; see https://osv.dev/vulnerability/GHSA-v845-jxx5-vc9f

Without the table, no advisory is looked up and nothing is fetched. The keys are in the reference, the rules in the rule catalog.

docs.title: Where the data comes from
docs.text:
The sources are the ones pixi sbom --vulns reads, read the same way, so both tools report the same advisories:

  • OSV for the advisories (GitHub's, the PyPI advisory database's and the rest), with their severity from the database's rating or the CVSS v3 vector, whichever is worse. Records about the same vulnerability, such as a GHSA and a PYSEC entry sharing a CVE, are one advisory.
  • CISA's KEV catalog for known-exploited. With known-exploited = "error" (the default), a known exploited advisory counts as critical, so it fails whatever fail-on is, and the message keeps its own rating: critical severity (rated medium), known exploited. With "warn" or "allow" its rating is left alone. An EPSS score does not change a rating.
  • FIRST's EPSS scores for epss, asked for only when epss is set. An advisory with several CVEs takes the highest score.

OSV has no conda ecosystem, so a conda package is looked up by its PyPI identity: the PyPI purls pixi.lock states for it, and, for a conda-forge package the lockfile states none for, the name conda-forge's conda-to-PyPI mapping gives it (the mapping pixi uses). pypi-mapping = "lock" uses the lockfile's purls only, as pixi sbom --vulns does by default; pixi sbom --vulns --pypi-mapping prefix matches the default here. A conda package with no PyPI identity, such as openssl, is not covered, and neither is a PyPI package built from a git checkout or a local path.

docs.title: Caching, offline use and mirrors
docs.text:
Answers are cached beside the extended policies: OSV's for an hour, its records until they change, the catalog, the scores and the mapping for a day. When a download fails, a stale copy stands in.

When the data cannot be read at all, because the network is down and nothing is cached or PIXI_POLICY_OFFLINE is set with an empty cache, advisories.unavailable fails the check: a gate that passes when it could see nothing would be worse than one that stops. To run offline in CI, run once online and keep PIXI_POLICY_CACHE_DIR in the CI cache.

On a network that blocks the public services, point these at mirrors that answer the same way:

Variable Default PIXI_POLICY_OSV_URL https://api.osv.dev PIXI_POLICY_KEV_URL https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json PIXI_POLICY_EPSS_URL https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss PIXI_POLICY_MAPPING_URL https://conda-mapping.prefix.dev/compressed-v0/compressed_mapping.json

docs.title: Accepting an advisory
docs.text:
A waiver with advisory accepts one advisory on one package, by its id or any alias:

[[waivers]]
rule = "advisories.vulnerable"
package = "urllib3"
advisory = "CVE-2023-43804"
reason = "no redirects to other origins; SEC-123"
expires = 2027-03-31

Without advisory, the waiver accepts every advisory on the package, including ones published after it was written.

docs.title: VEX statements
docs.text:
A VEX document says why an advisory does not affect a product. [advisories] vex names the ones the check reads:

[advisories]
vex = ["security/vex.cdx.json", "https://github.com/acme/policies/raw/v3/vendor.openvex.json"]

Each entry is a path relative to the policy file that names it, or a pinned https URL (a tag or a commit in it), fetched once and cached like an extended policy. A shared policy can carry its VEX: an entry in a base is found beside that base, by its path or relative to its URL, and every file's entries add up.

pixi-policy reads CycloneDX JSON (a VEX, or an SBOM with vulnerabilities[].analysis) and OpenVEX, as pixi-sbom's --vex-in does. A statement applies to an advisory finding when it names the advisory by its id or any alias, and names the package by a purl (pkg:pypi/urllib3@1.26.4; without a version, every version), or names no product at all. A conda package is matched by its own purl and by the PyPI purls it was looked up by. When several statements apply, the last one wins.

State OpenVEX status The finding not_affected, false_positive not_affected is waived, with the statement resolved, resolved_with_pedigree fixed is waived, with the statement exploitable, in_triage affected, under_investigation still fails

A waived finding is listed with the others, its statement in place of a waiver:

waived[advisories.vulnerable] urllib3 1.26.4: GHSA-v845-jxx5-vc9f (CVE-2023-43804), high severity: ... (pixi.lock: environment "default", linux-64); VEX: not_affected (code_not_reachable), vex.cdx.json: never parses cookies

In JSON the entry has vex (state, justification, detail, source) instead of waiver; in SARIF it is a suppressed result with the statement as its justification. A statement does not expire; a VEX file that cannot be read or is neither format stops the check with exit code 2.

docs.title: In development and CI
docs.text: The policy lives in the repository, so a laptop, a pre-commit hook and CI all check exactly the same rules. pixi-policy needs nothing running beside it: it reads pixi.toml, pixi.lock and the policy, and exits.

docs.title: What a run needs
docs.text:
• pixi.lock, committed. Every rule except the manifest ones reads it. Without a [lock] table, a missing lockfile is an input error (exit 2); with one, it is a lock.present finding.
  • pixi on PATH. lock.in-sync asks pixi, offline, whether the lockfile still satisfies the manifest (pixi list --locked). When pixi cannot be run, that check is a warning instead.
  • pixi-policy.toml, beside pixi.toml or named with --policy. A run without a policy is an error, never a pass.

docs.title: A pixi task
docs.text:
Pin pixi-policy with the workspace's other tools, in a feature that has Python, and give it a task:

# pixi.toml
[feature.lint.dependencies]
python = "3.12.*"

[feature.lint.pypi-dependencies]
pixi-policy = ">=0.1,<0.2"

[feature.lint.tasks]
policy = "pixi-policy"

[environments]
lint = { features = ["lint"], solve-group = "default" }

pixi run policy then runs the same version for everyone. Extra arguments pass through: pixi run policy --format json.

docs.title: Checking before you install
docs.text:
pixi lock cannot run anything after it solves, so pixi policy lock does the three steps in one:

pixi policy lock             # pixi lock, then check the new pixi.lock
pixi policy lock --install   # and pixi install --frozen once the check passes
pixi policy lock --restore   # and put the old pixi.lock back if the check fails
pixi policy lock -- --no-install   # arguments after -- go to pixi lock

By default a failing check leaves the new pixi.lock in place to look at, and exits 1 with the report; --restore puts the one from before back. Nothing is installed after a failing check.

It is a convenience, not a gate: pixi install, pixi run, pixi add and the other commands that lock re-lock an out-of-sync workspace without asking pixi-policy. The pre-commit hook and CI below are what keep a failing lockfile out of the repository.

docs.title: A pre-commit hook
docs.text:
The published hook runs the check whenever pixi.toml, pixi.lock, pyproject.toml or pixi-policy.toml changes, and stops a commit with an error finding:

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/aesir-oss/pixi-policy-pre-commit
    rev: v0.2.0
    hooks:
      - id: pixi-policy

Each tag of aesir-oss/pixi-policy-pre-commit installs the pixi-policy wheel of the same version from PyPI, so nothing is compiled; pre-commit autoupdate moves rev to the newest release. The hook checks the workspace the way pixi policy does from the repository root. args: passes any other flag: args: [--manifest-path, app/pixi.toml] for a workspace below the root.

To run the version the workspace pins instead (the pixi task above), a local hook:

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: pixi-policy
        name: pixi policy
        entry: pixi run policy
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
        files: (^|/)(pixi\.toml|pixi\.lock|pyproject\.toml|pixi-policy\.toml)$

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The GitHub Action is one step: it installs the release binary, runs the check, fails the job on an error finding and can upload the findings to code scanning.

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action@v0
  with:
    upload-sarif: "true"

The same by hand, with the version the workspace pins: write a SARIF report and upload it, so findings appear on the pull request as code scanning annotations at the line in pixi.toml, pixi.lock or the policy. The check's exit code fails the job; if: always() uploads the report even then.

# .github/workflows/policy.yml
name: Policy
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  policy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write   # upload-sarif
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: prefix-dev/setup-pixi@v0.8.1
        with:
          environments: lint
      - name: Check the policy
        run: pixi run policy --format sarif --output policy.sarif
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()
        with:
          sarif_file: policy.sarif
          category: pixi-policy

Make the job a required status check, or a failing policy is only advice. Code scanning is free on public repositories; private ones need GitHub code security. Without it, drop the upload and read the text report in the job log.

docs.title: Other CI systems
docs.text: Use the exit code to pass or fail the job, and --format json --output policy.json for anything that reads the results: a dashboard, a comment bot, an artifact to keep. The JSON report has a published schema.

docs.title: Who owns the policy
docs.text: Changing pixi-policy.toml changes what the workspace may contain, so review it like code: put it under CODEOWNERS, so a new waiver or a loosened rule needs its owner's approval.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
pixi-policy is one Rust crate. Everything runs through pixi, which pins the toolchain in pixi.lock, so a checkout builds the same way on every machine and in CI.

pixi run test   # unit and end-to-end tests
pixi run ci     # the full gate: pre-commit, release build, check, clippy, coverage >= 90%

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Task What it does test cargo test: the unit tests beside the code and the end-to-end tests in tests/ lint cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings check, fmt, build cargo check, cargo fmt, the release build cov coverage with cargo llvm-cov, failing under 90% of lines ci pre-commit-run, build, check, lint and cov: what must pass before a change is done policy-docs regenerate the policy reference and the rule catalog from the code -e lint deny cargo deny check: advisories, licenses, banned crates and sources, against deny.toml -e msrv msrv-check cargo check on the oldest toolchain Cargo.toml claims -e docs docs-serve, -e docs docs-build this site, served with live reload or built strictly -e rego rego-test opa test on the Rego example against pixi policy facts of an example workspace

pixi run bootstrap installs the pre-commit hooks once per clone.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Path What it is src/main.rs, src/cli.rs the command line src/check.rs, src/rules/ the rule engine and one module per rule family src/policy.rs, src/keys.rs the policy file's parser, and every key it accepts with its type, values and default src/lockfile.rs, src/manifest.rs, src/workspace.rs reading pixi.lock and pixi.toml src/license.rs, src/license_policy.rs, src/purl.rs license normalisation, the license verdict, package URLs src/report.rs, src/style.rs, src/pipe.rs text, JSON and SARIF reports; terminal colour; output a reader may close early src/explain.rs, src/waivers.rs, src/init.rs explain, waivers that expire, init src/vex.rs, src/facts.rs VEX statements for [advisories]; pixi policy facts schemas/ the JSON report's and the facts' schemas, published with the docs actions/pixi-policy/ the GitHub Action, copied to aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action on each release pre-commit-mirror/ the pre-commit hook, rendered into aesir-oss/pixi-policy-pre-commit on each final tests/ end-to-end tests of the binary, with fixtures and schemas examples/projects/pixi/ 19 real pixi workspaces the tests and the field test run against examples/rego/ built-in rules written in Rego over pixi policy facts, with opa test tests docs/, mkdocs.yml this site

The license, lockfile, purl, style and pipe modules began in a crate pixi-policy shared with pixi-sbom in aesir-oss/pixi-ext-contrib. Since this repository was split out, they are pixi-policy's own and change with its needs.

docs.title: Generated pages
docs.text: The policy reference and the rule catalog are generated from src/keys.rs and the text pixi policy explain prints. tests/docs.rs fails when either page differs from the code, and src/keys.rs has tests that fail when the policy parser accepts a key the reference does not list, or the reference lists one the parser rejects. Change the code, then run pixi run policy-docs.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
A release starts from the Release workflow (workflow_dispatch, with a version). It refuses to run unless main's CI passed on the commit, then bumps the version in Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and pixi.toml, adds the release's section to CHANGELOG.md with git-cliff, commits, and pushes the tag vX.Y.Z. The tag starts Release artifacts, which builds the wheels and the five archives (pixi-policy-vX.Y.Z-<platform>), signs their provenance, publishes the GitHub release, and uploads the wheels: to TestPyPI for a release candidate (0.1.1-rc.1), to PyPI for a final. Publishing the release redeploys this site under the version.

  • Never bump versions or push tags by hand: a pushed v* tag starts a release.
  • Never edit CHANGELOG.md's existing sections. Each release adds its own on top; those up to 0.1.0 were written in aesir-oss/pixi-ext-contrib and link there.
  • Every release candidate goes through a field test of the published files before a final is cut.

The same run fills two generated repositories with the release App, which must be installed on both:

  • aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action gets actions/pixi-policy/ on every release, tagged vX.Y.Z. A final also moves vX when it is the newest release of its major, and gets a GitHub release, marked Latest when vX moved: the Marketplace lists the action from releases, not tags.
  • aesir-oss/pixi-policy-pre-commit gets the hook rendered for the version, tagged vX.Y.Z, on finals only and after the PyPI upload, since the hook installs the wheel from PyPI.

The Marketplace listing itself is a manual step, once: GitHub has no API for it. On the first final's release in aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action, choose Edit, tick Publish this Action to the GitHub Marketplace (an aesir-oss owner may first have to accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement), pick the categories Security and Continuous integration, and update the release. The listing is marketplace/actions/pixi-policy.

docs.title: Sharing a policy
docs.text:
A platform team writes the policy once and every workspace builds on it, instead of copying a file that then drifts. A policy names the policies it builds on in [policy] extends:

# app/pixi-policy.toml
[policy]
extends = ["../policies/base.toml"]

[bans]
deny = [{ name = "pycrypto", use-instead = "pycryptodome" }]

Paths are relative to the file that names them. The bases apply in the order listed, each on top of the ones before, and the extending file last. A base may extend others in turn; a policy that ends up extending itself is an error, and a base reached twice is read once.

docs.title: Extending a URL
docs.text:
A base can also be a URL, as long as it is pinned, so the policy cannot change under a workspace without a commit to that workspace:

[policy]
extends = [
  # A tag or a commit in the URL pins it.
  "https://github.com/acme/policies/raw/v3/base.toml",
  # Anything else, or plain http, carries the sha256 of its content.
  { url = "https://intranet.example.com/policies/base.toml", sha256 = "9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08" },
]
  • A URL is pinned by a path segment that is a commit (40 hex digits) or a version tag (v3, 1.2.0). A branch such as main is not pinned, and an unpinned URL is an error. With a sha256, any URL works, http included, and content with another sha256 is refused.
  • A URL is fetched the first time it is needed and cached; after that the check reads the cache and needs no network. The cache is pixi-policy/ in pixi's cache directory, beside pixi-sbom's: $PIXI_CACHE_DIR or $RATTLER_CACHE_DIR when set, otherwise ~/.cache/rattler/cache on Linux (or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/rattler/cache), ~/Library/Caches/rattler/cache on macOS and %LOCALAPPDATA%\rattler\cache on Windows. PIXI_POLICY_CACHE_DIR moves it, for example into a CI cache.
  • PIXI_POLICY_OFFLINE=1 forbids the network: a base that is not cached is then an error instead of a fetch.
  • The fetch uses the system's certificate store, and a proxy from the first of ALL_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY that is set (in upper or lower case), skipping the hosts in NO_PROXY.
  • A relative path in a fetched base is read against its URL, and must itself be pinned: a base pinned by a tag or commit can extend its neighbours in the same tree, while one pinned only by its sha256 must name its own bases with theirs.

docs.title: Tighten anything, loosen only what the base allows
docs.text:
An extending policy may make anything stricter. It may loosen a value only when the base that set it lists the key in [policy] overridable:

# policies/base.toml
[policy]
overridable = ["licenses.allow"]

[licenses]
allow = ["MIT", "BSD-3-Clause", "Apache-2.0"]
deny = ["AGPL-*"]

Here a workspace may add a license to allow, but it cannot remove AGPL-* from deny or widen anything else the base sets. Loosening a key the base does not list stops the check with an error (exit 2) that names the key and the base. For a single package, a waiver is the way to loosen: it names the package, the reason and an expiry, and needs nothing from the base.

How each key combines is the When extended column of the policy reference:

When extended Keys What the extending file can do adds up [bans] deny, [licenses] deny and review, [manifest] required-platforms add entries; every file's entries apply and none can be removed may only narrow [sources] allowed-channels and allowed-indexes, [licenses] allow replace the list with one that allows no more than the base's may only be stricter [sources] allow-git, allow-url, allow-path, [licenses] unknown, the [manifest] and [lock] switches, max-waiver-days set a stricter value this file only [policy], [[waivers]] they are never inherited

Some details:

  • A table turns its rules on for every file after it. When the base has a [lock] table, a workspace that sets [lock] in-sync = false is loosening, even though the base never wrote in-sync.
  • With an allow list, an entry in [licenses] review is also acceptable, so adding a review entry the base's allow does not cover counts as loosening licenses.allow.
  • In a chain, a value is checked against every file that set it. A middle policy that lists a key in overridable lets the files after it loosen only its own value, never past a stricter value set further down that does not list the key.
  • Waivers stay with the file that holds them, and max-waiver-days from a base limits the extending file's waivers.

docs.title: What a policy resolves to
docs.text:
pixi policy show --resolved prints the merged policy, each value followed by the file it comes from, and marks each value a policy loosened under its base's overridable:

$ pixi policy show --resolved
# pixi-policy.toml, resolved: every policy it extends merged in, each value followed by the file it comes from.
# Read in order: ../policies/base.toml, pixi-policy.toml

[licenses]
allow = ["MIT", "BSD-3-Clause", "Apache-2.0", "PSF-2.0"]  # pixi-policy.toml, loosens ../policies/base.toml (overridable there)
deny = [
  "AGPL-*",  # ../policies/base.toml
]

pixi policy show without --resolved prints the policy file as written.

docs.title: Freshness
docs.text:
[freshness] fails a workspace that locks packages that are years old, far behind their newest release, or no longer maintained:

[freshness]
max-build-age-days = 730   # a build older than two years fails
max-majors-behind = 1      # a package two or more major versions behind its channel's newest fails
archived = true            # a conda-forge package whose feedstock is archived fails (on once the table exists)
pypi = true                # PyPI packages are checked too (on once the table exists)

error[freshness.majors-behind] setuptools 59.8.0: 25 major versions behind 84.0.0, the newest in conda-forge, more than max-majors-behind (1)
  --> pixi.lock: environment "default", linux-64
  = help: upgrade it, or waive it while the upgrade is planned

The keys are in the reference, the rules in the rule catalog. PyPI packages are checked against pypi.org; see PyPI packages.

docs.title: Build age
docs.text: max-build-age-days reads the build time each conda package's record in pixi.lock states, so it needs no network. A package whose record has no build time is reported as freshness.unknown.

docs.title: Major versions behind
docs.text:
max-majors-behind compares a package's major version, its leading number, with the newest release in the repodata of the channel pixi.lock installs it from: conda.anaconda.org, prefix.dev or a mirror, whichever the lockfile names. A mirror is therefore judged by its own contents, and a mirror that lags upstream does not fail a workspace for releases it cannot install yet.

  • The package's own subdir and noarch both count, since packages move between them: setuptools' linux-64 builds stop at 65, and its newer releases are noarch.
  • Prereleases do not count as the newest release.
  • A calendar-versioned package (2024.8.30) is compared by its year.
  • A package its channel's repodata does not list, or whose major version cannot be read, is freshness.unknown.

Repodata is read sharded where the channel serves it (CEP-16, as pixi does): a small index, then one shard per package. A channel that serves no shards is read whole, from repodata.json.zst or repodata.json, which for a large channel is a download of tens of megabytes the first time each day. No repodata is fetched unless max-majors-behind is set.

docs.title: Archived feedstocks
docs.text:
archived asks whether conda-forge has archived the feedstock that builds a conda-forge package: archived feedstocks get no new builds, so no fixes either. It reads two files the conda-forge bot publishes:

  • all_feedstocks.json from regro/cf-graph-countyfair, listing active and archived feedstocks;
  • feedstock-outputs.json from conda-forge/feedstock-outputs, naming the feedstocks that build each package.

The list can trail GitHub

The archived list is the bot's, regenerated from the conda-forge GitHub organization on each bot cycle, so a feedstock archived on GitHub shows up a few hours later, and a cached copy adds up to a day more. A feedstock unarchived on GitHub likewise keeps failing until the list and the cache catch up.

A package more than one feedstock builds counts as archived only when all of them are, since the lockfile does not say which one built it (libzlib comes from zlib or zlib-ng). A package no feedstock is known to build is freshness.unknown. Packages from other channels are not checked.

docs.title: PyPI packages
docs.text:
With pypi (on once the table exists), max-build-age-days and max-majors-behind apply to PyPI packages from pypi.org too, from PyPI's JSON API, one request per project:

  • Build age is when the exact file pixi.lock locks (matched by its sha256) was uploaded to PyPI. A file PyPI does not list is freshness.unknown.
  • The newest release is the newest PyPI lists by PEP 440 that is neither a prerelease nor yanked.
  • A package from another index, a URL, git or a path is freshness.unknown, as is a name PyPI has no project for.

pypi = false leaves PyPI packages out, as pixi-policy 0.2.0 did. archived is about conda-forge feedstocks and does not apply to PyPI. Nothing is fetched from PyPI unless one of the two limits is set.

error[freshness.majors-behind] pytest 7.0.0: 2 major versions behind 9.1.1, the newest on PyPI, more than max-majors-behind (0)
  --> pixi.lock: environment "test", linux-64
  = help: upgrade it, or waive it while the upgrade is planned

docs.title: Caching, offline use and mirrors
docs.text:
Answers are cached beside the extended policies: the shard index, a channel's whole repodata reduced to the newest version of each package, each PyPI project reduced to its newest release and upload times, and the feedstock lists for a day, shards for good (they are named by their content's hash). When a download fails, a stale copy stands in.

When the data cannot be read at all, because the network is down and nothing is cached or PIXI_POLICY_OFFLINE is set with an empty cache, freshness.unavailable fails the check; build ages are still judged, since they need no data. To run offline in CI, run once online and keep PIXI_POLICY_CACHE_DIR in the CI cache.

Repodata always comes from each package's own channel. The feedstock lists and PyPI's JSON API can come from mirrors:

Variable Default PIXI_POLICY_FEEDSTOCKS_URL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/regro/cf-graph-countyfair/master/all_feedstocks.json PIXI_POLICY_FEEDSTOCK_OUTPUTS_URL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/conda-forge/feedstock-outputs/single-file/feedstock-outputs.json PIXI_POLICY_PYPI_URL https://pypi.org (/pypi/<name>/json below it)

A waiver accepts a finding for one package, as for every rule.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Start from a policy the workspace already passes, commit it, and tighten it one change at a time. Each change is then a reviewed pull request that says exactly what is no longer allowed.

docs.title: 1. Write a starting policy
docs.text:
pixi policy init

init writes pixi-policy.toml beside pixi.toml from what the workspace uses today: the channels and indexes its packages come from, every license its packages declare (pixi.lock's, and the PyPI wheels' it can read), its platforms, the Python its environments resolve, and its own exclude-newer cooldown when it sets one. [advisories] and [freshness] are written commented out, since they use the network. It never overwrites an existing file; pass --policy <file> to write somewhere else.

# pixi-policy.toml, written by `pixi policy init` from what this workspace uses today.
[sources]
allowed-channels = ["conda-forge"]
allowed-indexes = ["https://pypi.org/simple"]
allow-git = false
allow-url = false
allow-path = false

[bans]
deny = []  # e.g. { name = "pycrypto", reason = "unmaintained", use-instead = "pycryptodome" }

[licenses]
# Every license the packages declare today: pixi.lock's, and the PyPI wheels' METADATA it could read. (Shortened here.)
allow = ["Apache-2.0", "BSD-3-Clause", "MIT", "PSF-2.0"]
unknown = "warn"

# Known vulnerabilities and freshness use the network; turn them on when it is there.
# [advisories]  # fails on high and critical advisories and known exploited ones
# [freshness]
# max-build-age-days = 730
# max-majors-behind = 1

[hygiene]  # no PyPI package duplicates a conda package today

[python]
version = "3.12"

[manifest]
required-platforms = ["linux-64", "osx-arm64", "win-64"]
# min-exclude-newer-days = 7  # with exclude-newer = "7d" in the workspace, a cooldown for new releases

[lock]  # present, complete and in-sync are all on

docs.title: 2. Check it
docs.text:
pixi policy

warning[licenses.unknown] python-dateutil 2.9.0.post0: license "Dual License" in its METADATA is not an SPDX expression (unknown term: 'Dual')
  --> pixi.lock: environment "docs", linux-64
  = help: find the license the package ships and waive this with it as the reason, or set [licenses] unknown = "allow" to stop these

0 errors, 10 warnings, 0 waived in 645 packages across 10 environment-platform pairs

Each finding names its rule, the package, where it was found and how to fix it. Errors fail the check (exit code 1); warnings are reported and do not. Commit pixi-policy.toml once the check passes.

docs.title: 3. Tighten it
docs.text:
Add what the workspace must never contain, one rule at a time:

[bans]
deny = [
  { name = "pycrypto", reason = "unmaintained", use-instead = "pycryptodome" },
  { name = "openssl", version = "<3", reason = "EOL" },
]

[licenses]
deny = ["GPL-3.0-*", "AGPL-*"]

pixi policy explain <RULE> says what a rule checks, gives an example and lists each of its keys with the values it takes and its default:

pixi policy explain bans.deny

docs.title: 4. Waive what has to stay, with an end date
docs.text:
When a finding cannot be fixed yet, waive that one finding with a reason and an expires date. It is reported as waived until then and fails again the day after.

[[waivers]]
rule = "licenses.deny"
package = "readline"
reason = "dev only; LEGAL-1234"
expires = 2027-03-31

See Waivers for how a waiver matches a finding.

docs.title: 5. Run it in CI
docs.text: Run the same check on every pull request, so a change to pixi.toml or pixi.lock that breaks the policy fails before it merges. In development and CI has the setup.

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text:
aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action runs pixi policy check in a workflow: it downloads the release binary for the runner, verifies its checksum, runs the check and fails the job when a finding is an error. pixi itself is not needed, though with pixi on PATH (from prefix-dev/setup-pixi) the lock.in-sync rule also runs; without it, that check is a warning.

# .github/workflows/policy.yml
name: Policy
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  policy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write   # upload-sarif
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action@v0
        with:
          upload-sarif: "true"

The text report goes to the job log and the job summary. With upload-sarif, findings also appear on the pull request as code scanning annotations at the line in pixi.toml, pixi.lock or the policy. Code scanning is free on public repositories; private ones need GitHub code security. Make the job a required status check, or a failing policy is only advice.

@v0 follows the newest 0.x.y release. Pin an exact release (@v0.2.0) or a commit sha for a build that never changes underneath you; version picks the binary independently of the ref.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Input Default What it does version the ref's pixi-policy version to run: @v0.2.0 runs 0.2.0, @v0 the newest 0.x.y, a branch the newest release manifest-path nearest pixi.toml The workspace's pixi.toml policy pixi-policy.toml beside it The policy to check against fail-on-findings true Fail the step on an error finding; with false it passes with a warning and failed says what happened summary true Write the text report to the job summary upload-sarif false Also write the report as SARIF and upload it to code scanning (needs security-events: write) sarif-category pixi-policy Code scanning category for the upload json-output Also write the JSON report to this path extra-args Additional command-line arguments, whitespace separated

A policy, manifest or lockfile that cannot be read (exit code 2) always fails the step, whatever fail-on-findings says.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Output What it is version The pixi-policy version that ran failed true when at least one finding is an error sarif Path of the SARIF report, when upload-sarif is set json Path of the JSON report, when json-output is set

docs.title: A workspace in a subdirectory
docs.text:
- uses: aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action@v0
  with:
    manifest-path: services/api/pixi.toml

Paths in the SARIF report are relative to the job's working directory, the repository root, so annotations land on the right files.

docs.title: A nightly re-check
docs.text:
When a waiver expires, the finding it waived fails the check again, with no commit to start a run. A scheduled run catches it:

on:
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"

docs.title: Report without failing
docs.text:
- uses: aesir-oss/pixi-policy-action@v0
  id: policy
  with:
    fail-on-findings: "false"
    json-output: policy.json
- if: steps.policy.outputs.failed == 'true'
  run: echo "the workspace fails its policy; see policy.json"

docs.title: License policy with pixi-policy
docs.text:
pixi-policy's [licenses] table is the policy-file form of pixi-sbom's license gate (--allow-license, --deny-license, --require-license). Both tools evaluate a license expression with the same verdict; pixi-policy also reads common non-SPDX spellings (see How a license string is read).

# pixi-policy.toml
[licenses]
allow = ["MIT", "BSD-3-Clause", "Apache-2.0", "PSF-2.0"]
review = ["LGPL-*"]
deny = ["GPL-3.0-*", "AGPL-*"]
unknown = "warn"     # or "error", "allow"
ambiguous = "warn"   # or "error", "allow"
Rule Severity Finds a package whose license… licenses.deny error cannot be satisfied without a deny license (MIT OR GPL-3.0-only passes: MIT is an option) licenses.not-allowed error cannot be satisfied with allow and review licenses alone (only when allow is given) licenses.review warning needs a review license licenses.unknown unknown is missing, or is not an SPDX expression licenses.ambiguous ambiguous is a name that could be more than one SPDX license (BSD, GPL, LGPL2, Apache)

An OR expression offers a choice, so a package passes when one option is acceptable: MIT OR GPL-3.0-only passes a policy that denies GPL-3.0-only. It needs a review when its only acceptable options are review licenses: Apache-2.0 OR BSD-2-Clause with allow = ["MIT"] and review = ["Apache-2.0"] is licenses.review, since BSD-2-Clause is not allowed.

Entries are SPDX identifiers, or patterns with * that are expanded against the SPDX license list (LGPL-* is every LGPL identifier). An -or-later entry accepts later versions of the same license, as in pixi-sbom.

docs.title: How a license string is read
docs.text:
A license that is an SPDX expression is used as it is. Common spellings that name one license are read as it from a reviewed table: BSD 3-Clause, New BSD License and 3-clause BSD License are BSD-3-Clause; Apache License 2.0 and ASL 2.0 are Apache-2.0; PSF and Python Software Foundation License are PSF-2.0; GPL-3 is GPL-3.0-only; LGPLv3+ is LGPL-3.0-or-later; Expat and MIT/X11 are MIT. A finding about such a package shows both, license PSF-2.0 (pixi.lock says "PSF") needs a review, so a reading can be checked.

A name that does not say which license it is (BSD, GPL, LGPL, LGPL2, BSD Like, a bare Apache) is never guessed at: it is licenses.ambiguous. Find the license the package ships and waive the finding with it as the reason, or ask the package's maintainers to state an SPDX license.

pixi-sbom's gate does not read this table yet, so a package spelt this way can pass one and be reported by the other.

docs.title: Moving from pixi-sbom's flags
docs.text: pixi-sbom pixi-policy --allow-license MIT --allow-license Apache-2.0 [licenses] allow = ["MIT", "Apache-2.0"] --deny-license GPL-3.0-only [licenses] deny = ["GPL-3.0-only"] --require-license [licenses] unknown = "error" no --require-license [licenses] unknown = "allow" (the default, "warn", reports them without failing) --ignore-license PACKAGE:WHY a waiver with a reason and an expiry date (no equivalent) [licenses] review = [...], reported as warnings exit code 3 on a violation exit code 1 on an error finding

docs.title: What pixi-policy reads
docs.text:
Conda licenses come from pixi.lock, offline. It records none for PyPI packages, so for a wheel from pypi.org pixi-policy reads the wheel's METADATA: its License-Expression (PEP 639), else a short License field, else a single License :: trove classifier that names one license (License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License is MIT; several classifiers, or BSD License alone, are licenses.ambiguous). It fetches only the end of the wheel with HTTP range requests, not the whole file, and caches what it read by the wheel's sha256, so the next run, or an offline one (PIXI_POLICY_OFFLINE), reads the cache. PIXI_POLICY_WHEEL_URL replaces https://files.pythonhosted.org with a mirror.

A source distribution, a wheel from another index, and a package from a URL, git or a path are not read: each is licenses.unknown, and the finding says why. So is a wheel whose METADATA cannot be read. pixi-sbom's gate also covers npm packages it reads from a package-lock.json (and licenses it fetches with --fetch-licenses); pixi-policy checks the packages in pixi.lock.

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
--format picks the report: text (the default), json or sarif. --output <file> writes it to a file instead of standard output. Whatever the format, the exit code is the verdict.

Code Meaning 0 Nothing failed. Warnings may still be reported 1 At least one finding is an error 2 The policy, the manifest or the lockfile could not be read

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
For people, in a terminal or a CI log. Findings are grouped by severity, each with its rule, the package, where it was found and a fix hint, then a summary line:

error[bans.deny] openssl 3.6.4: is banned (version <3): EOL
  --> pixi.lock: environment "default", linux-64
  = help: use libressl instead

1 error, 0 warnings, 0 waived in 1644 packages across 30 environment-platform pairs

--color auto (the default) colours it when standard output is a terminal and the environment does not forbid it; always colours it even when redirected (for less -R or a CI log), and never turns colour off. A report written with --output is never coloured unless --color always.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
For scripts and dashboards: one object per finding with stable field names, the waived findings with their waivers, and a summary.

{
  "version": 1,
  "tool": { "name": "pixi-policy", "version": "0.1.0" },
  "workspace": { "manifest": "pixi.toml", "lockfile": "pixi.lock", "policy": "pixi-policy.toml" },
  "summary": { "passed": false, "errors": 1, "warnings": 0, "waived": 0, "packages": 1644, "targets": 30 },
  "findings": [
    {
      "rule": "bans.deny",
      "severity": "error",
      "package": "openssl",
      "version": "3.6.4",
      "environment": "default",
      "platform": "linux-64",
      "file": "pixi.lock",
      "line": null,
      "message": "is banned (version <3): EOL",
      "help": "use libressl instead"
    }
  ],
  "waived": []
}

The schema is pixi-policy-report.schema.json. For the packages themselves rather than the findings, as input for another policy engine, see Facts for OPA and Rego. Fields may be added within version 1; renaming or removing one raises the version.

docs.title: SARIF
docs.text: SARIF 2.1.0, for GitHub code scanning and other SARIF viewers: one rule per rule ID, with the rule catalog's text as its help, and one result per finding at its file and line. Waived findings are included as suppressed results, so a viewer can show what was waived and why. In development and CI shows the upload.

docs.title: Policy file reference
docs.text: Every key pixi-policy.toml accepts. A key the table does not list is an error, so a misspelt key cannot quietly check nothing. pixi policy explain <RULE> prints the rows for one rule's keys. The When extended column says how a key combines when one policy extends another; see Sharing a policy.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text: Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules max-waiver-days integer 0 or more: the furthest a waiver's expires may be from today, in days; 0 turns the check off 365 no may only be stricter, unless overridable waivers.too-long

docs.title: [policy]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: the policy extends nothing, and nothing may loosen it.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [policy] extends list of strings or tables the policies this one builds on: a path relative to this file, an https URL pinned to a tag or commit ("https://github.com/acme/policies/raw/v3/base.toml"), or a table with url and sha256. They apply in order, then this file on top: it may tighten anything, and loosen only what they list in overridable []: the policy stands alone no this file only – [policy] extends: url string the policy's URL, http or https; fetched once and cached none yes – – [policy] extends: sha256 string the sha256 of the policy's content, 64 lower-case hex digits; a policy with another is refused none yes – – [policy] overridable list of strings IDs of keys a policy extending this one may loosen: the keys that may only narrow or be stricter ("licenses.allow", "sources.allow-git", "max-waiver-days") []: nothing this policy sets may be loosened no this file only –

docs.title: [sources]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no source rule runs.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [sources] allowed-channels list of strings channel names or URLs. A name ("conda-forge") matches its anaconda.org and prefix.dev URLs; any other host is given by URL ("https://conda.example.com/prod"). Trailing slashes and host case do not matter not set: conda packages may come from any channel no may only narrow, unless overridable sources.channels [sources] allowed-indexes list of strings PyPI index URLs ("https://pypi.org/simple"). Trailing slashes and host case do not matter not set: PyPI packages may come from any index no may only narrow, unless overridable sources.indexes [sources] allow-git boolean true, false true: packages may come from a git repository no may only be stricter, unless overridable sources.git [sources] allow-url boolean true, false true: packages may come from a direct URL no may only be stricter, unless overridable sources.url [sources] allow-path boolean true, false true: packages may come from a local path no may only be stricter, unless overridable sources.path

docs.title: [bans]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: nothing is banned.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [bans] deny list of tables one table per ban, with the fields below []: nothing is banned no adds up bans.deny [bans] deny: name string a package name. A PyPI name also catches a conda package that provides it none yes – bans.deny [bans] deny: version string a version range: conda's syntax for conda packages, PEP 440 for PyPI ones ("<3", ">=1.0,<1.1.1w") not set: every version is banned no – bans.deny [bans] deny: build string a conda build-string pattern, with * matching any run of characters ("*_cuda*"); conda packages only not set: every build is banned no – bans.deny [bans] deny: kind string "conda", "pypi" not set: both kinds no – bans.deny [bans] deny: reason string any text; printed with the finding none no – bans.deny [bans] deny: use-instead string any text; printed as the finding's fix hint none no – bans.deny

docs.title: [licenses]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no license rule runs.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [licenses] allow list of strings SPDX license identifiers, or patterns with * expanded against the SPDX license list ("LGPL-*"). An -or-later entry accepts later versions of the same license []: any license that is not denied is acceptable no may only narrow, unless overridable licenses.not-allowed [licenses] review list of strings SPDX license identifiers or patterns, as for allow [] no adds up licenses.review, licenses.not-allowed [licenses] deny list of strings SPDX license identifiers or patterns, as for allow [] no adds up licenses.deny [licenses] unknown string "warn", "error", "allow" "warn" no may only be stricter, unless overridable licenses.unknown [licenses] ambiguous string "warn", "error", "allow": what a license name that could be more than one SPDX license gets "warn" no may only be stricter, unless overridable licenses.ambiguous

docs.title: [advisories]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no advisory rule runs, and nothing is fetched.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [advisories] fail-on string "low", "medium", "high", "critical": an advisory at or above it fails "high" once the table exists no may only be stricter, unless overridable advisories.vulnerable [advisories] known-exploited string "error", "warn", "allow": what an advisory in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog gets, whatever its severity; with "error" it counts as critical "error" once the table exists no may only be stricter, unless overridable advisories.vulnerable [advisories] epss float a probability from 0 to 1: an advisory whose EPSS score (FIRST's estimate that it is exploited in the next 30 days) is at or above it fails not set: EPSS scores are not asked for no may only be stricter, unless overridable advisories.vulnerable [advisories] unknown string "warn", "error", "allow": what an advisory with no severity gets "warn" no may only be stricter, unless overridable advisories.unknown [advisories] pypi-mapping string "prefix": a conda package is looked up by the PyPI purls pixi.lock states for it or, when it states none, by conda-forge's conda-to-PyPI mapping; "lock": by pixi.lock's purls only "prefix" no may only be stricter, unless overridable advisories.vulnerable, advisories.unknown [advisories] vex list of strings CycloneDX or OpenVEX JSON files, by a path relative to the policy that names them or a pinned https URL: an advisory a statement marks not_affected, false_positive or resolved for a package is waived with it [] no adds up advisories.vulnerable, advisories.unknown

docs.title: [freshness]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no freshness rule runs, and nothing is fetched.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [freshness] max-build-age-days integer 0 or more: a conda package built more days ago than this fails, by the build time pixi.lock records not set: build age is not checked no may only be stricter, unless overridable freshness.build-age, freshness.unknown [freshness] max-majors-behind integer 0 or more: a conda package whose major version is more than this far behind the newest release in its channel's repodata fails not set: versions are not compared, and no repodata is fetched no may only be stricter, unless overridable freshness.majors-behind, freshness.unknown, freshness.unavailable [freshness] archived boolean true, false: a conda-forge package whose feedstock conda-forge has archived fails true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable freshness.archived, freshness.unknown, freshness.unavailable [freshness] pypi boolean true, false: PyPI packages from pypi.org are checked too, by the locked file's upload time and the newest release PyPI lists true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable freshness.build-age, freshness.majors-behind, freshness.unknown, freshness.unavailable [freshness] unknown string "warn", "error", "allow": what a package gets when the data says nothing about it "warn" no may only be stricter, unless overridable freshness.unknown

docs.title: [hygiene]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no hygiene rule runs.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [hygiene] conda-pypi-duplicate boolean true, false: a PyPI package a conda package in the same environment already provides fails true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable hygiene.conda-pypi-duplicate, hygiene.unavailable

docs.title: [python]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no python rule runs.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [python] version string a minor version, "3.14": the Python every environment runs; any patch release of it matches none yes may only be stricter, unless overridable python.older, python.newer, python.requires-python [python] older string "error", "warn", "allow": what an environment whose Python is an older minor version gets "error" no may only be stricter, unless overridable python.older [python] newer string "warn", "error", "allow": what an environment whose Python is a newer minor version gets "warn" no may only be stricter, unless overridable python.newer [python] requires-python boolean true, false: the pyproject's [project] requires-python must not admit an older minor than version, and must admit version false no may only be stricter, unless overridable python.requires-python

docs.title: [manifest]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no manifest rule runs.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [manifest] wildcard-spec boolean true, false true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable manifest.wildcard-spec [manifest] python-pinned boolean true, false true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable manifest.python-pinned [manifest] required-platforms list of strings pixi platform names ("linux-64", "linux-aarch64", "osx-64", "osx-arm64", "win-64", …) not set: no platform is required no adds up manifest.required-platforms [manifest] min-exclude-newer-days integer 0 or more: the shortest cooldown the workspace's exclude-newer, and each per-package override, may give not set: exclude-newer is not checked no may only be stricter, unless overridable manifest.exclude-newer

docs.title: [lock]
docs.text:
A table. When it is left out: no lock rule runs, and a missing pixi.lock is an input error (exit 2).

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [lock] present boolean true, false true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable lock.present [lock] complete boolean true, false true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable lock.complete [lock] in-sync boolean true, false true once the table exists; without the table the rule is off no may only be stricter, unless overridable lock.in-sync

docs.title: [[waivers]]
docs.text:
A list of tables. When it is left out: no exceptions.

Key Type Allowed values Default Required When extended Rules [[waivers]] rule string the ID of a policy rule, as pixi policy explain lists it ("licenses.deny"); waivers.* findings cannot be waived none yes – waivers.unused [[waivers]] package string the package's name, as the finding names it (case does not matter). Findings that name no package, such as the lock rules', cannot be waived none yes – waivers.unused [[waivers]] version string an exact version, as the finding names it not set: every version no – waivers.unused [[waivers]] environment string an environment name from pixi.toml not set: every environment no – waivers.unused [[waivers]] platform string a pixi platform name ("linux-64") not set: every platform no – waivers.unused [[waivers]] advisory string an advisory's id or any of its aliases ("GHSA-…", "PYSEC-…", "CVE-…"), as the finding lists them; advisories.* waivers only not set: every advisory on the package no – waivers.unused [[waivers]] reason string any text: why the exception is acceptable, and until when none yes – – [[waivers]] expires date a TOML date, YYYY-MM-DD, unquoted: the last day the waiver applies none yes – waivers.expired, waivers.too-long

docs.title: Facts for OPA and Rego
docs.text:
An organization that already writes its policy in Rego can give OPA what pixi-policy knows about a workspace, rather than learn a second policy language:

pixi policy facts --output facts.json
opa eval --input facts.json --data policy.rego "data.pixi.policy.deny"

pixi policy facts reads pixi.lock, and for PyPI wheels from pypi.org their licenses as the license rules do (cached, offline from the cache), and writes every environment and platform it locks with their packages. The shape is pixi-policy-facts.schema.json, versioned like the JSON report: fields may be added, and a renamed or removed field raises version.

{
  "version": 1,
  "tool": { "name": "pixi-policy", "version": "0.3.0" },
  "workspace": { "manifest": "pixi.toml", "lockfile": "pixi.lock" },
  "environments": [
    {
      "name": "default",
      "platform": "linux-64",
      "packages": [
        {
          "name": "readline",
          "version": "8.3",
          "kind": "conda",
          "purl": "pkg:conda/readline@8.3?build=hd6e31c0_1&channel=conda-forge&subdir=linux-64&type=conda",
          "provides_pypi": [],
          "origin": { "type": "channel", "url": "https://conda.anaconda.org/conda-forge/", "channel": "conda-forge" },
          "license": { "declared": "GPL-3.0-only", "source": "pixi.lock", "spdx": "GPL-3.0-only", "status": "spdx" },
          "build": "hd6e31c0_1",
          "build_number": 1,
          "timestamp": 1787033801,
          "subdir": "linux-64",
          "sha256": "01b3fe073a66e321970d09e04b388708f8cbdca5cdfbfcb7c9eeb470ad10383d",
          "requires_python": null
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Field What it holds kind conda (an archive from a channel or URL), conda-source (built from source by pixi-build) or pypi origin.type channel, index, git, url or path: where the package comes from, as the sources.* rules see it provides_pypi the PyPI distributions pixi.lock states a conda package provides (conda msgpack-python provides msgpack) license.spdx the SPDX expression pixi-policy reads the declared license as, through its table of spellings license.source pixi.lock, wheel (a PyPI wheel's METADATA) or null when there is none license.status spdx, text (not an SPDX expression), ambiguous or missing

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
examples/rego/pixi.rego writes three of the built-in rules in Rego:

package pixi.policy

settings := {
    "allowed_channels": {"conda-forge"},
    "banned": {"py"},
    "denied_licenses": {"GPL-3.0-only"},
}

packages contains [env.name, env.platform, pkg] if {
    some env in input.environments
    some pkg in env.packages
}

deny contains {"rule": "sources.channels", "package": pkg.name, "environment": env, "platform": platform} if {
    some [env, platform, pkg] in packages
    pkg.origin.type == "channel"
    not pkg.origin.channel in settings.allowed_channels
}

deny contains {"rule": "bans.deny", "package": pkg.name, "environment": env, "platform": platform} if {
    some [env, platform, pkg] in packages
    pkg.name in settings.banned
}

deny contains {"rule": "licenses.deny", "package": pkg.name, "environment": env, "platform": platform} if {
    some [env, platform, pkg] in packages
    pkg.license.spdx in settings.denied_licenses
}

It finds what this pixi-policy.toml finds, except that its license rule compares single identifiers where pixi-policy evaluates whole SPDX expressions:

[sources]
allowed-channels = ["conda-forge"]

[bans]
deny = [{ name = "py" }]

[licenses]
deny = ["GPL-3.0-only"]

CI runs the example's tests with opa test against the facts of an example workspace, and checks they expect what pixi-policy's own rules find there: pixi run -e rego rego-test locally.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Every rule pixi policy check runs, with the text pixi policy explain <RULE> prints. Each rule's keys are in the policy file reference.

Rule Checks sources.channels Conda packages come only from the channels the policy allows sources.indexes PyPI packages come only from the indexes the policy allows sources.git No package comes from a git repository unless the policy allows it sources.url No package comes from a direct URL unless the policy allows it sources.path No package comes from a local path unless the policy allows it bans.deny No package, or package version, the policy bans licenses.deny No package needs a license the policy denies licenses.review Packages that need a license under review are reported for it licenses.not-allowed Every package can be used under the licenses the policy allows licenses.unknown Every package declares an SPDX license licenses.ambiguous No package's license is a name that could be more than one SPDX license advisories.vulnerable A package has a known vulnerability at or above fail-on, known exploited, or above the EPSS threshold advisories.unknown A package has a known vulnerability whose severity no advisory gives advisories.unavailable The advisory data cannot be read, so no package could be checked freshness.build-age A package was built, or uploaded to PyPI, longer ago than max-build-age-days freshness.majors-behind A package is more major versions behind its channel's or PyPI's newest than allowed freshness.archived A conda-forge package comes from an archived feedstock freshness.unknown The channel or PyPI data says nothing about a package a freshness rule checks freshness.unavailable The channel or PyPI data cannot be read, so no package could be checked for freshness python.older No environment runs a Python older than the policy's standard python.newer No environment runs a Python newer than the policy's standard python.requires-python The pyproject's requires-python starts at the policy's standard Python and admits it hygiene.conda-pypi-duplicate No PyPI package is one a conda package in the same environment provides hygiene.unavailable conda-forge's PyPI mapping cannot be read, so some conda packages were not compared manifest.wildcard-spec No dependency is given as \* manifest.python-pinned Python is constrained to one minor version or narrower manifest.required-platforms The workspace lists every platform the policy requires manifest.exclude-newer exclude-newer keeps packages out for at least min-exclude-newer-days lock.present The workspace has a pixi.lock lock.complete Every environment is locked for every platform it is solved for lock.in-sync pixi.lock still satisfies the manifest waivers.expired A waiver has expired, and what it waived fails again waivers.unused A waiver matches no finding waivers.too-long A waiver runs further out than max-waiver-days

docs.title: sources.channels
docs.text:
Conda packages come only from the channels the policy allows.

Key: [sources] allowed-channels, a list of channel names or URLs. A name ("conda-forge") matches its anaconda.org and prefix.dev URLs only; any other host is listed by URL. Mirrors are matched as the channel they mirror, since pixi.lock records that channel.

[sources]
allowed-channels = ["conda-forge", "https://conda.example.com/prod"]

Keys: [sources] allowed-channels.

docs.title: sources.indexes
docs.text:
PyPI packages come only from the indexes the policy allows.

Key: [sources] allowed-indexes, a list of PyPI index URLs (trailing slashes and host case do not matter). pixi.lock records a wheel's index; one from the default index is checked against it.

[sources]
allowed-indexes = ["https://pypi.org/simple"]

Keys: [sources] allowed-indexes.

docs.title: sources.git
docs.text:
No package comes from a git repository unless the policy allows it.

Key: [sources] allow-git (default: allowed). Set it to false to fail any package, conda (pixi-build) or PyPI, that comes from a git repository.

[sources]
allow-git = false

Keys: [sources] allow-git.

docs.title: sources.url
docs.text:
No package comes from a direct URL unless the policy allows it.

Key: [sources] allow-url (default: allowed). Set it to false to fail any package that comes from a direct URL: an archive, not a channel or an index.

[sources]
allow-url = false

Keys: [sources] allow-url.

docs.title: sources.path
docs.text:
No package comes from a local path unless the policy allows it.

Key: [sources] allow-path (default: allowed). Set it to false to fail any package that comes from a local path, including a workspace package pixi builds from source.

[sources]
allow-path = false

Keys: [sources] allow-path.

docs.title: bans.deny
docs.text:
No package, or package version, the policy bans.

Key: [bans] deny, a list of bans: name, and optionally version (conda's rules for conda packages, PEP 440 for PyPI ones), build (a conda build-string pattern), kind ("conda" or "pypi"), reason and use-instead. A ban on a PyPI name also catches a conda package that provides it.

[bans]
deny = [
  { name = "pycrypto", reason = "unmaintained", use-instead = "pycryptodome" },
  { name = "openssl", version = "<3", reason = "EOL" },
]

Keys: [bans] deny, [bans] deny: name, [bans] deny: version, [bans] deny: build, [bans] deny: kind, [bans] deny: reason, [bans] deny: use-instead.

docs.title: licenses.deny
docs.text:
No package needs a license the policy denies.

Key: [licenses] deny, SPDX identifiers or patterns ("GPL-3.0-*"). A package fails when its license cannot be satisfied without a denied license: MIT OR GPL-3.0-only passes, since MIT is an option. The verdict is the one pixi-sbom's --deny-license gives.

[licenses]
deny = ["GPL-3.0-*", "AGPL-*"]

Keys: [licenses] deny.

docs.title: licenses.review
docs.text:
Packages that need a license under review are reported for it.

Key: [licenses] review, SPDX identifiers or patterns. A package that needs one is reported as a warning; review licenses count as allowed for licenses.not-allowed.

[licenses]
review = ["LGPL-*"]

Keys: [licenses] review.

docs.title: licenses.not-allowed
docs.text:
Every package can be used under the licenses the policy allows.

Key: [licenses] allow. When given, a package fails unless its license can be satisfied with allow and review licenses alone. An -or-later requirement accepts later versions of the same license.

[licenses]
allow = ["MIT", "BSD-3-Clause", "Apache-2.0"]

Keys: [licenses] allow, [licenses] review.

docs.title: licenses.unknown
docs.text:
Every package declares an SPDX license.

Key: [licenses] unknown = "warn" (default), "error" or "allow": what a package with no license, or one that is not an SPDX expression, gets. pixi.lock records no PyPI licenses; a wheel from pypi.org has its METADATA read (by range requests, cached by sha256), and a source distribution or a package from another index, a URL, git or a path stays unknown.

[licenses]
unknown = "error"

Keys: [licenses] unknown.

docs.title: licenses.ambiguous
docs.text:
No package's license is a name that could be more than one SPDX license.

Key: [licenses] ambiguous = "warn" (default), "error" or "allow": what a package gets whose license is a name that could be more than one SPDX license (BSD, GPL, LGPL2, Apache), rather than a guess at one. Common spellings that name one license (BSD 3-Clause, Apache License 2.0, PSF) are read as it from a reviewed table, and a finding about such a package shows what pixi.lock says.

[licenses]
ambiguous = "error"

Keys: [licenses] ambiguous.

docs.title: advisories.vulnerable
docs.text:
A package has a known vulnerability at or above fail-on, known exploited, or above the EPSS threshold.

Keys: [advisories] fail-on (default "high"), known-exploited (default "error") and epss (not set by default). A package fails for each advisory at or above fail-on, in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, or with an EPSS score at or above epss. With known-exploited = "error", a known exploited advisory counts as critical, its own rating kept in the message. Advisories are OSV's, as pixi-sbom --vulns reads them; a conda package is looked up by its PyPI identity (pypi-mapping). The help names the version that fixes it. Waive one advisory with a waiver's advisory key, or take it out with a VEX statement from a file [advisories] vex names (CycloneDX or OpenVEX: not_affected, false_positive and resolved are waived with it).

[advisories]
fail-on = "high"
known-exploited = "error"
epss = 0.1

Keys: [advisories] fail-on, [advisories] known-exploited, [advisories] epss, [advisories] pypi-mapping, [advisories] vex.

docs.title: advisories.unknown
docs.text:
A package has a known vulnerability whose severity no advisory gives.

Key: [advisories] unknown = "warn" (default), "error" or "allow": what an advisory gets when no record of it gives a severity or a CVSS v3 vector, unless known-exploited or epss already fail it.

[advisories]
unknown = "error"

Keys: [advisories] unknown, [advisories] pypi-mapping, [advisories] vex.

docs.title: advisories.unavailable
docs.text:
The advisory data cannot be read, so no package could be checked.

Key: [advisories]. The advisory data could not be read: OSV, CISA's catalog, FIRST's EPSS API or the conda-forge mapping did not answer and nothing was cached, or PIXI_POLICY_OFFLINE is set and the cache is empty. The check fails rather than pass a workspace it could not look at. PIXI_POLICY_OSV_URL, PIXI_POLICY_KEV_URL, PIXI_POLICY_EPSS_URL and PIXI_POLICY_MAPPING_URL point at mirrors.

[advisories]

Keys: .

docs.title: freshness.build-age
docs.text:
A package was built, or uploaded to PyPI, longer ago than max-build-age-days.

Key: [freshness] max-build-age-days (not set by default). Fails a conda package built more days ago than the limit, by the build time its record in pixi.lock states: no network. With pypi (on by default), a PyPI package from pypi.org fails when the file pixi.lock locks was uploaded longer ago, by PyPI's JSON API. A package with no build or upload time is freshness.unknown.

[freshness]
max-build-age-days = 730

Keys: [freshness] max-build-age-days, [freshness] pypi.

docs.title: freshness.majors-behind
docs.text:
A package is more major versions behind its channel's or PyPI's newest than allowed.

Key: [freshness] max-majors-behind (not set by default). Fails a conda package whose major version (the leading number) is more than the limit behind the newest release in the repodata of the channel and subdir pixi.lock names for it, so a mirror is judged by its own contents. With pypi (on by default), a PyPI package from pypi.org is compared with the newest release PyPI lists. Prereleases, and yanked PyPI releases, do not count as newest.

[freshness]
max-majors-behind = 1

Keys: [freshness] max-majors-behind, [freshness] pypi.

docs.title: freshness.archived
docs.text:
A conda-forge package comes from an archived feedstock.

Key: [freshness] archived (on once [freshness] exists). Fails a conda-forge package when every feedstock that builds it is archived, by the conda-forge bot's feedstock list, which can trail an archival on GitHub by a bot cycle (hours).

[freshness]
archived = true

Keys: [freshness] archived.

docs.title: freshness.unknown
docs.text:
The channel or PyPI data says nothing about a package a freshness rule checks.

Key: [freshness] unknown = "warn" (default), "error" or "allow": what a package gets when a freshness rule cannot judge it: no build time in pixi.lock, not in its channel's repodata, no major version to compare, no feedstock known to build it, or a PyPI package from somewhere other than pypi.org or whose locked file PyPI does not list.

[freshness]
unknown = "error"

Keys: [freshness] max-build-age-days, [freshness] max-majors-behind, [freshness] archived, [freshness] pypi, [freshness] unknown.

docs.title: freshness.unavailable
docs.text:
The channel or PyPI data cannot be read, so no package could be checked for freshness.

Key: [freshness]. The channel's repodata, conda-forge's feedstock lists or PyPI's JSON API could not be read: the network is down and nothing is cached, or PIXI_POLICY_OFFLINE is set and the cache is empty. The check fails rather than pass packages it could not look at.

[freshness]

Keys: [freshness] max-majors-behind, [freshness] archived, [freshness] pypi.

docs.title: python.older
docs.text:
No environment runs a Python older than the policy's standard.

Keys: [python] version, the standard minor version, and older = "error" (default), "warn" or "allow". Reports an environment whose Python, as pixi.lock resolves it for each platform, is an older minor version than the standard. Every patch release of the standard matches it; an environment without Python is not checked.

[python]
version = "3.14"
older = "error"

Keys: [python] version, [python] older.

docs.title: python.newer
docs.text:
No environment runs a Python newer than the policy's standard.

Keys: [python] version, the standard minor version, and newer = "warn" (default), "error" or "allow". Reports an environment whose Python, as pixi.lock resolves it for each platform, is a newer minor version than the standard. Every patch release of the standard matches it; an environment without Python is not checked.

[python]
version = "3.14"
newer = "error"

Keys: [python] version, [python] newer.

docs.title: python.requires-python
docs.text:
The pyproject's requires-python starts at the policy's standard Python and admits it.

Keys: [python] version and requires-python = true (false by default, since a library may support older Pythons on purpose). Reads [project] requires-python from the workspace's pyproject.toml, the manifest itself or one beside pixi.toml, and fails when it admits a Python minor older than the standard (>=3.12 with version = "3.14") or does not admit the standard at all (<3.14). Nothing is checked without a pyproject.toml or without requires-python.

[python]
version = "3.14"
requires-python = true

Keys: [python] version, [python] requires-python.

docs.title: hygiene.conda-pypi-duplicate
docs.text:
No PyPI package is one a conda package in the same environment provides.

Key: [hygiene] conda-pypi-duplicate (on once [hygiene] exists). Fails a PyPI package whose distribution a conda package in the same environment already provides, so both are installed one over the other. A conda package provides the PyPI names pixi.lock states purls for (conda msgpack-python is PyPI msgpack); for a conda-forge package it states none for, conda-forge's mapping gives them, read only when an environment has such a package and PyPI packages too.

[hygiene]
conda-pypi-duplicate = true

Keys: [hygiene] conda-pypi-duplicate.

docs.title: hygiene.unavailable
docs.text:
conda-forge's PyPI mapping cannot be read, so some conda packages were not compared.

Key: [hygiene]. conda-forge's conda-to-PyPI mapping could not be read: the network is down and nothing is cached, or PIXI_POLICY_OFFLINE is set and the cache is empty. The packages pixi.lock states PyPI names for are still compared; the check fails rather than pass the others. PIXI_POLICY_MAPPING_URL points at a mirror.

[hygiene]

Keys: [hygiene] conda-pypi-duplicate.

docs.title: manifest.wildcard-spec
docs.text:
No dependency is given as *.

Key: [manifest] wildcard-spec (on once [manifest] exists). Fails a conda or PyPI dependency given as "*" in any dependency table, at its line in the manifest.

[manifest]
wildcard-spec = true

Keys: [manifest] wildcard-spec.

docs.title: manifest.python-pinned
docs.text:
Python is constrained to one minor version or narrower.

Key: [manifest] python-pinned (on once [manifest] exists). Fails a python dependency whose spec allows more than one minor version (">=3.10"), or has none; "3.12.*" and ">=3.12,<3.13" pass.

[manifest]
python-pinned = true

Keys: [manifest] python-pinned.

docs.title: manifest.required-platforms
docs.text:
The workspace lists every platform the policy requires.

Key: [manifest] required-platforms, a list of platforms the workspace must list in [workspace] platforms.

[manifest]
required-platforms = ["linux-64", "osx-arm64"]

Keys: [manifest] required-platforms.

docs.title: manifest.exclude-newer
docs.text:
exclude-newer keeps packages out for at least min-exclude-newer-days.

Key: [manifest] min-exclude-newer-days (not set by default). Fails a workspace that sets no exclude-newer, or one whose cooldown is shorter: a duration ("7d", "1h30m", as pixi reads them) shorter than the minimum, or a date or timestamp fewer days ago (a date means the start of the next day, UTC, as pixi reads it). A per-package override in [exclude-newer] or [pypi-exclude-newer] that is shorter is its own finding, at its line. Most malicious uploads are found and removed within days, and a cooldown keeps them out of a solve.

[manifest]
min-exclude-newer-days = 7

Keys: [manifest] min-exclude-newer-days.

docs.title: lock.present
docs.text:
The workspace has a pixi.lock.

Key: [lock] present (on once [lock] exists). Fails a workspace without a pixi.lock; without [lock], a missing lockfile is an input error (exit 2) instead.

[lock]
present = true

Keys: [lock] present.

docs.title: lock.complete
docs.text:
Every environment is locked for every platform it is solved for.

Key: [lock] complete (on once [lock] exists). Fails an environment the manifest defines that pixi.lock does not lock, or does not lock for one of its platforms.

[lock]
complete = true

Keys: [lock] complete.

docs.title: lock.in-sync
docs.text:
pixi.lock still satisfies the manifest.

Key: [lock] in-sync (on once [lock] exists). Asks pixi, offline, whether pixi.lock still satisfies the manifest (pixi list --locked); a warning when pixi cannot be run.

[lock]
in-sync = true

Keys: [lock] in-sync.

docs.title: waivers.expired
docs.text:
A waiver has expired, and what it waived fails again.

A [[waivers]] entry whose expires date has passed. What it waived fails again; renew it with a new date and a reason that still holds, or fix the finding.

[[waivers]]
rule = "licenses.deny"
package = "readline"
reason = "dev only; LEGAL-1234"
expires = 2027-03-31

Keys: [[waivers]] expires.

docs.title: waivers.unused
docs.text:
A waiver matches no finding.

A [[waivers]] entry that matches no finding: its rule, package, version, environment or platform is wrong, or the finding is gone. Remove it.

[[waivers]]
rule = "bans.deny"
package = "pycrypto"
reason = "replaced in Q3"
expires = 2027-01-31

Keys: [[waivers]] rule, [[waivers]] package, [[waivers]] version, [[waivers]] environment, [[waivers]] platform, [[waivers]] advisory.

docs.title: waivers.too-long
docs.text:
A waiver runs further out than max-waiver-days.

A [[waivers]] entry whose expires is more than max-waiver-days (default 365) away. The waiver still applies. Set max-waiver-days at the top of the policy; 0 turns the check off.

max-waiver-days = 180

Keys: max-waiver-days, [[waivers]] expires.

docs.title: Waivers
docs.text:
A waiver is an exception for one rule and one package, with a reason and an end date. The waived finding is still reported, as waived, and does not fail the check. The day after expires, it fails again.

[[waivers]]
rule = "licenses.deny"
package = "readline"
reason = "dev only; LEGAL-1234"
expires = 2027-03-31

docs.title: What a waiver matches
docs.text:
A waiver covers a finding when its rule and package match the finding's (the package name ignoring case), and each of version, environment and platform that it gives matches too. Leave those out to cover every version, environment and platform:

[[waivers]]
rule = "bans.deny"
package = "openssl"
version = "1.1.1w"
environment = "legacy"
platform = "linux-64"
reason = "the legacy environment ships to RHEL 7 until it is retired"
expires = 2026-12-31

Only findings about a package can be waived. The lock rules name no package; turn one off with its key ([lock] in-sync = false) instead. The findings about waivers themselves (waivers.*) cannot be waived.

docs.title: Every waiver ends
docs.text:
expires is required, as a TOML date, YYYY-MM-DD, unquoted. The policy reports three things about waivers, all as warnings at the waiver's line in the policy:

Rule When What to do waivers.expired expires has passed; what it waived fails again fix the finding, or renew the waiver with a new date and a reason that still holds waivers.unused it matches no finding remove it, or correct its rule, package, version, environment or platform waivers.too-long expires is more than max-waiver-days away (365 by default) bring expires closer, or raise max-waiver-days

max-waiver-days sets how far out a waiver may run; it is a top-level key, so it goes above the first table. 0 turns the check off:

max-waiver-days = 180

[licenses]
deny = ["GPL-3.0-*"]

docs.title: Moving from pixi-sbom's --ignore-license
docs.text: pixi-sbom's --ignore-license PACKAGE:WHY has no end date. Write each one as a waiver of licenses.deny (or licenses.not-allowed) for that package, with the reason and a date to look at it again.
